sources.entry: Python: _Just enough of a Git client to create a repo, commit, and push itself to GitHub_

summary.title: pygit: Just enough of a Git client to create a repo, commit, and push itself to GitHub
summary.one_liner: You learn how Git's object database, binary index, tree and commit objects, and smart HTTP push protocol work by walking through a ~500-line Python implementation that pushes itself to GitHub.
takeaways: Git's local object database is plain zlib-compressed files under .git/objects, addressed by SHA-1 of a header plus content.
Trees list mode, name and binary hash of entries recursively, and commits point to a tree and parent commit, so each commit is a full directory snapshot.
The .git/index file is a custom binary format with a 12-byte header, 62-byte fixed entry fields plus padded path, and a trailing SHA-1 checksum.
Pushing over GitHub's smart HTTP protocol requires pkt-line framing and sending a PACK file of the objects the remote lacks, which the author built with only the Python standard library.
summary.summary: The author describes pygit, about 500 lines of Python 3.5+ using only the standard library, that implements init, add, commit, and push plus status, diff, cat-file, ls-files, and hash-object. The article walks through each part of the code: hashing and storing objects, reading and writing the binary index, building tree and commit objects, the pkt-line format, a urllib-based authenticated HTTPS request, computing missing objects, and creating an undeltified pack file for git-receive-pack. It contrasts the project with Mary Rose Cook's gitlet, noting that pygit pushes to a real remote server and uses the binary index format so output can be checked against git.
